Description: explicit — GeoJSON vs tiles decision for a real scenario
prompt: I have about 8,000 hiking trail segments stored as GeoJSON, and users need to click a trail to see its name and distance. I also need a basemap showing terrain and roads. How should I set up the data sources in MapLibre — do I need vector tiles, or can I use GeoJSON?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer** *Use a hosted vector-tile basemap for terrain + roads and add your 8 000 trail segments as a separate **GeoJSON source**. If the GeoJSON file stays under ~5 MB (or you can simplify it to that size) you’ll be fine on desktop and most mobiles. If the file grows larger or you notice a 1-2 s pause when the map first loads, switch the trails to a tiny vector-tile set (tippecanoe → PMTiles or a TileJSON endpoint).* Below is a step-by-step rationale, the exact thresholds you should check, and a ready-to-copy code example. --- ## 1️⃣ Why a **two-source pattern** is the right architecture | Layer | What it does | Why it’s a separate source | |------|--------------|----------------------------| | **Basemap** (terrain + roads) | Provides context, labels, hill-shade, elevation data. | Usually a *vector* tileset that you don’t control; you just point to a style URL (e.g. MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, or a self-hosted vector style). | | **Trails overlay** | Interactive line features that you want to query (click → name + distance). | You own the data, you want full client-side access to properties, and you only have ~8 k features. Keeping it separate means you can edit the GeoJSON without rebuilding the whole basemap. | MapLibre can request any number of sources in parallel; there is **no per-source rendering penalty**. The “one source” myth (merge everything into one tileset) only makes sense for an offline kiosk where you must ship a single file. For a normal web app the two-source pattern is simpler, cheaper, and far more flexible. --- ## 2️⃣ GeoJSON vs. vector tiles for 8 000 trail segments | Metric | GeoJSON (inline / URL) | Vector tiles | |--------|------------------------|--------------| | **Typical file size** | 1 – 4 MB if you simplify (see § 2.3) | < 200 KB for the same data (compressed PBF) | | **Load-time** | One HTTP request, then full parse in the browser. | One request per tile (usually 2-6 tiles in view) → < 200 ms total. | | **Interactivity** | Full feature properties available client-side. | Same, but you need to `querySourceFeatures` or `feature-state`. | | **Update workflow** | Just replace the GeoJSON file (or fetch fresh data via API). | Regenerate tiles whenever geometry changes (tippecanoe/Planetiler). | | **Complexity** | Zero server side – just host a static .geojson file. | Requires a tile server or static PMTiles host. | | **Thresholds** (from the skill) | • **Sweet spot**: < 2 MB / < 5 000 features – instant.
• **Lag zone**: 5-20 MB / up to ~50 000 features – 1-3 s parse, mobile may stutter.
• **Crash zone**: > 50 MB / > 100 000 features – risk of freeze. | Works comfortably for any size; the only limit is tile-generation time. | **Your numbers** * 8 000 line features → well above the “< 5 000” sweet-spot count, but the *size* is what really matters. * A typical trail line (average ~200 m) with a few properties (name, length, difficulty) is ~200 bytes per vertex. Even with 10 vertices per segment you’re looking at ~16 KB per feature → ~128 MB raw – far too big. * However, if you **simplify** (reduce vertices, drop unnecessary properties, round coordinates to 5-6 decimal places) you can usually bring the file down to **2-4 MB**. **Conclusion:** *Start with GeoJSON.* If after simplifying the file stays **≤ 5 MB** you’ll be in the “lag zone” at worst – still acceptable for most desktop browsers and many mobiles. Test it; if you see a noticeable pause or memory spike, move the trails to a tiny vector-tile set. --- ## 3️⃣ How to keep the GeoJSON file small enough | Technique | How to apply | Approx. impact | |-----------|--------------|----------------| | **Coordinate precision** | `JSON.stringify(geojson, null, 0).replace(/\d\.\d{6,}/g, m => Number(m).toFixed(6))` or use `geojson-rewind` + `geojson-precision` npm packages. | Cuts size ~30 % | | **Vertex reduction** | Run `mapshaper -simplify 10%` (or a tolerance that keeps the trail shape recognizable). | 40-70 % depending on original density | | **Drop unused properties** | Keep only `name`, `distance`, maybe `difficulty`. | 10-30 % | | **Compress on the wire** | Serve the file with gzip/brotli (most CDNs do this automatically). | 70-80 % transfer reduction (no effect on parse time). | | **Chunked loading (optional)** | If you still need to stay under 2 MB, split the trails into logical groups (e.g., by region) and load the appropriate GeoJSON on demand. | Reduces initial payload, adds a little code. | If after these steps the file is still > 5 MB, go to the vector-tile path (next section). --- ## 4️⃣ Vector-tile alternative (quick-start) 1. **Generate tiles** (one-time step) ```bash # Install tippecanoe (brew, apt, or from source) tippecanoe \ --output=trails.pmtiles \ --layer=trails \ --minimum-zoom=5 \ --maximum-zoom=14 \ --drop-densest-as-needed \ --simplify-only-low-zoom \ trails.geojson ``` *Tip:* `--drop-densest-as-needed` keeps the tile size < 200 KB automatically. 2. **Host the PMTiles** (static file on a CDN, or use the serverless `pmtiles` endpoint). Example CDN URL: `https://cdn.example.com/tiles/trails.pmtiles` 3. **Add a `vector` source** in your style: ```json { "id": "trails", "type": "vector", "url": "pmtiles://https://cdn.example.com/tiles/trails.pmtiles" } ``` (If you don’t want the `pmtiles://` protocol, you can serve a TileJSON that points to the same file.) 4. **Add a line layer** that references the source-layer `trails`. ```javascript map.addLayer({ id: 'trail-lines', type: 'line', source: 'trails', 'source-layer': 'trails', paint: { 'line-color': '#006400', 'line-width': [ 'interpolate', ['linear'], ['zoom'], 5, 1, 12, 3, 14, 5 ] } }); ``` 5. **Interactivity** – query the vector source on click: ```javascript map.on('click', 'trail-lines', (e) => { const props = e.features[0].properties; new maplibregl.Popup() .setLngLat(e.lngLat) .setHTML(`${props.name}
Length: ${props.distance} km`) .addTo(map); }); ``` That pipeline gives you sub-second loading, works on low-end phones, and still lets you style the trails dynamically. --- ## 5️⃣ Putting it all together – final code snippet (GeoJSON path) ```html Trails on a terrain basemap
``` **Key points in the snippet** * **Basemap** is a *vector* style URL that already includes terrain (`terrain` source) and road layers. * **`firstSymbolId`** ensures your trail lines are drawn **under** the basemap’s label symbols, keeping text readable. * **Click handler** reads the GeoJSON properties directly—no extra server round-trip. * **Performance tip:** Serve the GeoJSON with gzip/brotli and set `Cache-Control` headers so the browser caches it. --- ## 6️⃣ When to switch to vector tiles (quick checklist) | Condition | Action | |-----------|--------| | Final GeoJSON size **> 5 MB** after simplification | Generate a small vector-tile set (tippecanoe → PMTiles) and replace the `geojson` source with a `vector` source. | | Mobile users report “long pause” or “browser freezes” on map load | Same as above; vector tiles guarantee sub-second load. | | You want **different styling per zoom** (e.g., thicker lines at high zoom, simplified geometry at low zoom) without re-generating GeoJSON each time | Vector tiles let you use `line-width` expressions that depend on `zoom`. | | You plan to **add more data later** (e.g., 20 k+ new trail segments) | Build a tile pipeline now; adding new features is just a new tippecanoe run. | If you hit any of those, the migration is straightforward: ```javascript map.addSource('trails', { type: 'vector', url: 'pmtiles://https://cdn.example.com/tiles/trails.pmtiles' }); ``` …and keep the same layer definition (just add `'source-layer': 'trails'`). --- ## 7️⃣ TL;DR checklist for your project 1. **Simplify & compress** the 8 000-segment GeoJSON. *Target size ≤ 5 MB.* 2. **Use a hosted vector-tile basemap** that includes terrain (MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, etc.). 3. **Add the trails as a separate `geojson` source** (as shown in the full example). 4. **Insert the trail layer before the first symbol layer** so labels stay on top. 5. **

Description: implicit — dataset outgrew GeoJSON without the user naming tiles
prompt: My parcel layer is a 180 MB GeoJSON file with around 400,000 polygons. The browser hangs for ages on load and sometimes the tab just dies. I've already tried minifying the JSON. What now?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR Your 180 MB / ≈ 400 k-polygon GeoJSON is well beyond the **GeoJSON “crash zone”** ( > 50 MB / > 100 k features ). The browser has to download **the whole file**, parse it into JavaScript objects, and then hand every vertex to WebGL – that’s why it hangs or dies. **The only practical fix is to stop using a single GeoJSON source and switch to a tiled format** (vector tiles are the usual choice; raster tiles are an alternative only if you don’t need interactivity). Below is a step-by-step plan that takes you from the current GeoJSON to a production-ready MapLibre map, with the minimal amount of extra infrastructure. --- ## 1. Why GeoJSON Won’t Work Any More | Metric | GeoJSON “sweet spot” | Your data | What happens | |--------|----------------------|-----------|--------------| | File size | < 2 MB | **180 MB** | Full download → long network time + huge memory pressure | | Feature count | < 5 k | **≈ 400 k** | Browser must keep 400 k objects + all vertices in RAM | | Parse time | < 0.5 s | 1–3 s + possible freeze | Main thread blocked → UI hangs, mobile may kill the tab | | Interaction | Fast (click/hover) | **Unusable** | No time to build feature index, map freezes on pan/zoom | Even aggressive minification or “pretty-print-off” does not change the fact that **the whole dataset is transferred and parsed**. The only way to keep the map responsive is to **serve only the data that is actually visible** – that’s exactly what tiled sources do. --- ## 2. Choose the Right Tile Type | Need | Recommended source type | Why | |------|------------------------|-----| | Interactive polygons, need click/hover, styling changes, occasional updates | **Vector tiles (`type: "vector"` )** | Geometry + attributes stay client-side, you can query features, style on the fly, and keep file size tiny (often < 10 KB per tile). | | Pure visual background, no interaction needed | **Raster tiles (`type: "raster"` )** | Simpler to generate, but you lose feature-level interactivity. | | Offline kiosk / single-file bundle | **PMTiles** (a single archive that contains vector tiles) | Still vector-tile based, but packaged as one file; see the *maplibre-pmtiles-patterns* skill. | > **Bottom line:** For a polygon layer you want to click or style, go with **vector tiles**. --- ## 3. Turn Your GeoJSON into Vector Tiles You don’t have to build a full tile server from scratch – a few command-line tools can generate a ready-to-serve tile set in minutes. | Tool | When to use | Quick command (example) | |------|-------------|--------------------------| | **tippecanoe** (Felt) | Small-to-medium GeoJSON (up to a few hundred MB) – fast, simple, works on any OS. | ```bash tippecanoe \
--output=data.mbtiles \
--layer=parcels \
--drop-densest-as-needed \
--simplify-only-low-zoom \
--maximum-zoom=14 \
--no-feature-limit \
parcels.geojson``` | | **Planetiler** (onthegomap) | Very large datasets, need fine-grained control, or want to generate multiple layers from the same source. | ```bash java -jar planetiler.jar \
--input parcels.geojson \
--output data.mbtiles \
--maxzoom 14 \
--simplify 0.5``` | | **ogr2ogr → MVT** | You already have the data in a spatial database (PostGIS, SQLite) and want to stream tiles on demand. | ```bash ogr2ogr -f MVT data.mvt parcels.geojson -lco MAXZOOM=14 -lco MINZOOM=0``` | **Key tip-offs while generating tiles** | Option | What it does | Why you need it for 400 k polygons | |--------|--------------|-----------------------------------| | `--drop-densest-as-needed` (tippecanoe) | Removes vertices from the most detailed tiles when the tile would otherwise exceed the size limit (default 500 KB). | Keeps tile size manageable without you having to manually simplify. | | `--simplify-only-low-zoom` | Applies aggressive simplification at low zooms, preserving detail only where you zoom in. | Prevents the low-zoom tiles from blowing up to megabytes. | | `--maximum-zoom` (or `--maxzoom`) | Sets the highest zoom level you’ll ever need. | If you never need > 14, you can stop at that level and drastically reduce tile count. | | `--no-feature-limit` | Disables the default 200 k feature per tile limit (tippecanoe). | Useful if a single tile still contains many small parcels; the tool will instead split the tile into a deeper zoom level. | | `--layer=parcels` | Gives the source-layer a stable name you’ll reference in the style. | Needed for `source-layer` in MapLibre layers. | After the command finishes you’ll have an **MBTiles** file (SQLite container of vector tiles). That file can be served in three common ways: 1. **Static HTTP tiles** – unzip the MBTiles to a folder structure (`/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`) and serve with any static web server (nginx, Apache, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages, etc.). 2. **PMTiles archive** – run `pmtiles convert data.mbtiles data.pmtiles` and serve the single file via a CDN or the built-in PMTiles server (see the *maplibre-pmtiles-patterns* skill). 3. **Tile server** – use a lightweight server like **tileserver-gl**, **tileserver-php**, or **t-rex** that reads MBTiles on demand. > **You don’t need a full-blown tile-rendering stack** unless you also want raster basemaps. The vector-tile approach works with a static file host or a tiny Node/Python server. --- ## 4. Wire the Vector Tile Source into MapLibre Below is a minimal style snippet that adds your new vector tile source **and** keeps a basemap (e.g. OpenStreetMap vector tiles) separate. ```javascript // 1️⃣ Add a basemap (any hosted vector style) map.addSource('basemap', { type: 'vector', url: 'https://api.maptiler.com/maps/streets-v2/style.json?key=YOUR_KEY' // or your own TileJSON URL }); // 2️⃣ Add your parcel tiles (served as /tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf) map.addSource('parcels', { type: 'vector', tiles: ['https://my.cdn.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf'], // optional: minzoom / maxzoom if you limited them during generation minzoom: 0, maxzoom: 14 }); // 3️⃣ Add a fill layer for the parcels map.addLayer({ id: 'parcel-fill', type: 'fill', source: 'parcels', 'source-layer': 'parcels', // matches the layer name you set when tiling paint: { 'fill-color': '#ff6600', 'fill-opacity': 0.4 } }); // 4️⃣ Add an outline (optional) map.addLayer({ id: 'parcel-outline', type: 'line', source: 'parcels', 'source-layer': 'parcels', paint: { 'line-color': '#222', 'line-width': 1 } }); ``` **Important ordering tip** – if you want your parcels to appear *under* the basemap’s label symbols, insert the layers **before** the first symbol layer in the style: ```javascript const firstSymbol = map.getStyle().layers.find(l => l.type === 'symbol'); map.addLayer(parcelFill, firstSymbol.id); // inserts before labels ``` That way the labels stay readable. --- ## 5. Optional: Reduce Geometry Before Tiling (Extra Safety) If you still see very large tiles after the first pass, you can pre-simplify the GeoJSON **once** (outside of tippecanoe) to shrink the vertex count dramatically: ```bash # Using mapshaper (Node or binary) mapshaper parcels.geojson \ -simplify dp 10% keep-shapes \ -proj wgs84 \ -o parcels_simplified.geojson ``` - `dp` = Douglas-Peucker algorithm. - `10%` keeps 10 % of the original vertices (adjust as needed). - The resulting file will be far smaller, and tippecanoe will produce even lighter tiles. > **Do not** rely on client-side simplification; it still requires the full dataset to be transferred first. --- ## 6. When Raster Tiles Might Be Acceptable If you **don’t need** per-parcel click/hover or dynamic styling, you could render the polygons once on the server (e.g. with GDAL, QGIS, or MapServer) and publish them as **raster tiles** (PNG/WebP). That eliminates the need for vector-tile generation but also removes interactivity. The workflow is: 1. Render the GeoJSON to a raster image at each zoom level (e.g. `gdal2tiles.py`). 2. Serve the resulting `{z}/{x}/{y}.png` tiles. 3. Add a raster source in MapLibre: ```javascript map.addSource('parcels-raster', { type: 'raster', tiles: ['https://my.cdn.com/raster/{z}/{x}/{y}.png'], tileSize: 256 }); map.addLayer({ id: 'parcels-raster', type: 'raster', source: 'parcels-raster' }); ``` Only choose this route if you are okay with a **static image** and no feature queries. --- ## 7. Quick Checklist – What to Do Next | ✅ | Action | |---|--------| | 1 | **Simplify** the GeoJSON (optional) with `mapshaper` or `ogr2ogr -simplify`. | | 2 | **Generate vector tiles** with `tippecanoe` (or `planetiler` if you need more control). | | 3 | **Host the tiles** – either as a static folder (`/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`) or as a PMTiles archive. | | 4 | **Add the source** to your MapLibre style (see code snippet). | | 5 | **Insert layers** before the first symbol layer to keep labels on top. | | 6 | **Test** on desktop and mobile; you should see sub-second tile loads and smooth pan/zoom. | | 7 | If you need **offline** support, convert the MBTiles to PMTiles and use the *maplibre-pmtiles-patterns* skill to load it directly from the browser. | --- ## 8. Further Reading / Related Skills | Skill | What you’ll learn | |-------|-------------------| | **maplibre-pmtiles-patterns** | How to serve a single PMTiles file (perfect for kiosks or demos). | | **maplibre-source-wiring** | Detailed guide on TileJSON, `source-layer`, CORS, and debugging missing tiles. | | **maplibre-fonts-glyphs** | Setting up `glyphs` URLs if you need custom text rendering on top of your vector tiles. | | **maplibre-sprites-icons** | Adding custom icons (e.g., parcel markers) on top of your vector layer. | --- ### TL;DR Summary *Your 180 MB GeoJSON is far beyond what browsers can handle.* **Solution:** Convert the data to **vector tiles** (tippecanoe → MBTiles → static or PMTiles host) and add it as a separate `vector` source alongside any basemap you like. Description: anti-pattern — merging basemap and application data into one tileset
prompt: I want my roads, water, labels, and my own delivery-zone polygons all in a single vector tileset so the map only hits one source. What's the best pipeline to merge OpenStreetMap data with my polygons and build that combined tileset?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer – don’t merge everything into one tileset unless you have a very special offline-only use case.** For virtually every web-map you’ll get a better, more maintainable, and cheaper solution by keeping the basemap (roads, water, labels, etc.) as a **separate vector source** and adding your delivery-zone polygons as a second source (GeoJSON or its own vector tiles). MapLibre can request both sources in parallel, there is no per-source rendering penalty, and you keep the basemap up-to-date without rebuilding it every time your polygons change. Below is the recommended pattern, followed by the *only* scenario where a single combined tileset makes sense and a high-level pipeline you could use if you really need it. --- ## 1️⃣ Recommended “two-source” pattern | Source | Type | What it holds | Why it’s the right choice | |--------|------|---------------|---------------------------| | **Basemap** | `vector` (TileJSON URL) | Global OSM-derived layers: roads, water, land, place-name labels, etc. | Hosted basemap services (MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, Planet, etc.) already provide these layers at global scale, are updated regularly, and are covered by their own attribution/licensing. | | **Your data** | `geojson` **or** `vector` | Delivery-zone polygons (and any future custom layers) | • If you have < 5 000 polygons → a simple `geojson` source is fine (no tile server needed).
• If you exceed the GeoJSON sweet-spot (≈ 2 MB / 5 000 features) → generate a small vector-tile set just for your polygons. | **How to wire them in a style** ```javascript // 1️⃣ Basemap (hosted vector tiles) map.addSource('basemap', { type: 'vector', url: 'https://api.maptiler.com/maps/streets-v2/style.json?key=YOUR_KEY' // or any TileJSON URL }); // 2️⃣ Your delivery zones (choose one of the two options) // Option A – tiny dataset, keep it as GeoJSON map.addSource('delivery-zones', { type: 'geojson', data: '/data/delivery-zones.geojson' }); // Option B – larger dataset, pre-tile it map.addSource('delivery-zones', { type: 'vector', url: 'pmtiles://https://example.com/delivery-zones.pmtiles' // or TileJSON URL }); // 3️⃣ Add layers – insert your polygon layer *before* the first symbol layer // so your zones sit under road/label symbols. const firstSymbolId = map.getStyle().layers.find(l => l.type === 'symbol').id; map.addLayer({ id: 'zones-fill', type: 'fill', source: 'delivery-zones', 'source-layer': 'zones', // name you gave when tiling paint: { 'fill-color': '#ff6600', 'fill-opacity': 0.3 } }, firstSymbolId); ``` **Benefits** * **Zero extra build work** for the basemap – you just consume an existing style URL. * **Fast iteration** – change a polygon, re-upload the GeoJSON (or a tiny vector tile bundle) and the map updates instantly. * **Correct attribution** – you keep the basemap provider’s attribution separate and don’t have to redistribute OSM data yourself. * **Scalable** – the basemap can serve the whole world, while your custom source can be as small or as large as you need. --- ## 2️⃣ When a single combined tileset *is* justified A single tileset makes sense only for: * **Offline / air-gapped deployments** (e.g., a kiosk, a field-device, a demo that must run without any network connection). * **One-off proof-of-concepts** where you want to ship a single archive and don’t care about future updates. Even in those cases you’ll still end up with two logical layers inside the same tileset (one layer for the basemap, one for your polygons). The “single source” you’re after is really “a single *tileset file* that contains multiple layers”. ### High-level pipeline (no step-by-step code) 1. **Obtain the OSM base data** you need. * For a global or continental extent, download an OSM extract (e.g., from Geofabrik). * For a smaller region, you can use an overpass query or a pre-generated extract. 2. **Prepare your delivery-zone polygons** in GeoJSON (or any format tippecanoe can read – e.g., GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf). 3. **Merge the two datasets** into a single GeoJSON/Parquet collection, keeping distinct feature types separate (e.g., give OSM features a `layer` property like `roads`, `water`, `labels`; give your polygons a `layer` of `delivery_zones`). * You can do this with a simple script (Node.js, Python, or GDAL/OGR). * **Important:** keep the attribute schema tidy – OSM features have many tags; you may want to filter to only the tags you actually need for styling (highway, waterway, name, etc.) to keep tile size down. 4. **Tile the merged data** * **Tippecanoe** – the classic tool for turning large GeoJSON (or GeoParquet) into Mapbox-compatible vector tiles. Example command (adjust zoom range and layer names): ```bash tippecanoe \ --output=combined.mbtiles \ --layer=roads --filter='properties.highway' \ --layer=water --filter='properties.natural=="water"' \ --layer=labels --filter='properties.name' \ --layer=delivery_zones --filter='properties.zone_id' \ --minimum-zoom=0 --maximum-zoom=14 \ --drop-densest-as-needed \ merged.geojson ``` * **Planetiler** – a Java-based pipeline that can ingest OSM PBF directly and add custom layers from other sources. It’s more scalable for planet-size builds but requires a Java runtime and a bit more configuration. See its README for the `--extra-data` flag to add your polygons. 5. **Serve the tiles** * **PMTiles** – package the `.mbtiles` into a single static file and serve it with the `pmtiles://` protocol (MapLibre has built-in support). * **TileServer-GL**, **tileserver-php**, **tileserver-go**, or any static-file server that can expose the TileJSON endpoint. 6. **Create a style JSON** that references the single source and defines separate `source-layer` names (`roads`, `water`, `labels`, `delivery_zones`). The style can be built manually or with tools like **MapLibre Style Spec Builder**. 7. **Deploy** – copy the style JSON, the PMTiles file (or TileJSON endpoint), and any glyph/sprite assets to your static host or CDN. ### Caveats of the single-tileset approach | Issue | Why it matters | |-------|----------------| | **Re-building cost** | Any change to your polygons forces a full re-tile of the entire merged dataset (including the basemap). For a global OSM extract this can take hours. | | **Attribution/licensing** | By redistributing OSM data you become a *derivative* distributor and must carry OSM’s attribution and any other data source’s license. | | **Loss of basemap updates** | You’ll be stuck with the snapshot you built; you won’t get new roads, name changes, or bug fixes unless you rebuild. | | **File size** | A combined global MBTiles can be several hundred megabytes (or > 1 GB for high-detail zoom levels). That defeats the “single source = low bandwidth” goal for most web apps. | | **Complexity** | You now have to maintain a tile-generation pipeline, a CI/CD step, and storage for the large MBTiles file. | Because of these drawbacks, the **two-source pattern** is almost always the right answer for a typical web application. --- ## 3️⃣ Quick decision checklist | Your situation | Recommended approach | |----------------|----------------------| | < 5 000 polygons, want instant updates | **GeoJSON source** + hosted basemap vector source | | 5 000–100 000 polygons, acceptable 1–3 s load | **GeoJSON** (if you can simplify) **or** small **vector-tile source** for your polygons | | > 100 000 polygons **or** > 50 MB GeoJSON | **Vector-tile source** for your polygons (tippecanoe/Planetiler) + hosted basemap | | Must run completely offline, ship a single file | **Single combined MBTiles/PMTiles** (pipeline above) – but still keep layers separate inside the file | | Want to avoid any tile-generation work | Use a **hosted basemap** (MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, etc.) and a **GeoJSON** overlay | --- ## 4️⃣ TL;DR – What you should do today 1. **Pick a hosted vector basemap** (MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, etc.) and add it to your style. 2. **Add your delivery-zone polygons** as a `geojson` source if they’re under the sweet-spot; otherwise generate a tiny vector-tile set with **tippecanoe** (or **Planetiler** if you already have an OSM pipeline). 3. Insert your polygon layer before the first symbol layer so labels stay on top. 4. Deploy the style, glyphs, and sprites; you now have a fast, maintainable map that hits **two** sources (which is perfectly fine and the standard practice). If you later discover you truly need an offline-only single file, follow the high-level pipeline in section 2, but keep in mind the rebuild and licensing costs. --- **References used** * Tippecanoe – * Planetiler – * PMTiles spec – * MapLibre Style Spec – * OSM data extracts – Feel free to ask for more details on any step (e.g., a minimal tippecanoe command, how to filter OSM tags, or how to set up a PMTiles endpoint). Happy mapping!

prompt: My app is built on Leaflet and I want to add a MapLibre-style vector tile basemap to it. Is that possible, and how?
